brief.head: Friends of choice
brief.text: Amit Varma was a loner until early adulthood. The internet gave him communities of choice: he and Ajay Shah, both in Bombay, met online, though not on a dating app. {118-S08}

brief.head: The easy exit
brief.text: One student told a survey, Amit Varma recalled, that she used apps rather than date a classmate she might later see every day “with another girl”. {118-S09}

brief.head: Same age in public
brief.text: Studies say women seek men their own age. A friend told Amit Varma that was for appearances; privately, she prefers men much older or much younger. {118-S10}

brief.head: Lost in the manosphere
brief.text: Twenty-five years ago Amit Varma read Neil Strauss’s *The Game*, a pickup artists’ handbook. Its world is now an industry, and many of its men have given up on love. {118-S11}

brief.head: The great mystery
brief.text: Georges Simenon, one of Amit Varma’s favourite novelists, said the theme running through all his work was that no person can fully communicate himself to another. {118-J22}

thought.text: If you are not your authentic self, you can never be truly loved.
thought.who: Amit Varma, on what hiding our secret selves costs us; he thinks Paul Graham may have said it

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on men, women and data
lead.head: Dance like no one’s searching
body: Ask people what they want and you get their stated preferences. Watch what they type into a search box, or whom they swipe right on, and you see something closer to the truth.
That was the bet as Amit Varma and Ajay Shah turned their passion for measurement on men and women.

The subject was split off from their previous episode on data, which, Shah said, “would have been five hours” on its own. Inside the team, he added, Varma is known as the Energiser Bunny, “because he goes on and on”.
## Who is choosing?
Varma began with an old column of his, which argued that India’s rising divorce rates were “a damn good thing”: more women had the agency to leave bad marriages.
A friend, Hamsini Hariharan, had suggested a stranger metric still. More women in prison, Varma said, means more women with agency and the opportunity to go out in the world. {118-C01}
The test, the hosts agreed, is who really decides. A man who downloads a grocery app may simply hand the phone to his wife and pay for whatever she picks.
## The secret self

The heart of the episode was Seth Stephens-Davidowitz’s *Everybody Lies*, which Varma called a phenomenal book. Its premise is that people are most truly themselves when searching online, because they are anonymous and nobody is watching.
Varma invoked Gabriel García Márquez’s three selves: a public self, a private self known to a few intimates, and a secret self known “to nobody except Google Baba”. {118-C03}

That secret self, the data suggests, frets most about sex. Searches for “sexless marriage” far outnumber those for “unhappy marriage”, and parents are likelier than the childless to confess regret to Google.
Shah drew a broader lesson. The hosts live in a bubble, he said, whereas “this data reflects the median Indian”, who is “a very different person from us”.
## Swipe right, then what?

Dating apps, Varma argued, moved romance from communities of circumstance, fixed by geography, school and work, to communities of choice. “If you are a gay person say born in 1960, you could spend your whole life alone,” he said. One born in 2000 is not going to. {118-C08}

Choice has also brought inequality. Women swipe right on far fewer profiles than men, so a few men get most of the attention. Varma cited a Tinder Gini coefficient of 0.58, “more inequality than 95 per cent of the countries in the world”. {118-C09}

Shah asked what had changed, since desire has probably not altered in 65,000 years. Varma’s answer was that with a million profiles to choose from, everyone becomes super selective. “The instincts were always the same because they are what they are, but the behaviours have changed.”
Shah saw a lesson for measurement. A satellite photographing North Korea at night changes nothing there. Dating apps made romance observable and “completely changed the system as well”.

Finally, the hosts turned to a Facebook index of friendship between the sexes, which *The Economist* proposed to name after *When Harry Met Sally*. India scored 0.35. Shah called the separation of men and women in India “a social crisis”. {118-C15}
Varma closed on a larger mystery. Many economists, he said, are working on the wrong things. “We don’t understand ourselves. We don’t understand other people.”

second.label: Search and politics
second.head: Word order wins the vote
second.deck: Amit Varma on how Google searches read America’s voters before the polls did
body: Donald Trump’s rise in 2016 took many people aback. But Amit Varma, retelling the work of Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, said Google had seen it coming four years earlier: many searched for a racial slur alongside Obama’s victory, instead of “first black president”, in the states that later voted a particular way. {#trump}

After the most recent US election, Stephens-Davidowitz wrote in *The Economist* that a look at Google beat all the surveys on the television news. In states where people searched for the “Trump Harris debate”, Trump won. Where they searched for the “Harris Trump debate”, Harris won. {118-S05}
No person would think to look for such a signal, Varma said, but machines unleashed on the data find it.

quote.text: Just that word order. And it’s such a subtle thing.

second.caption: Google and the Trump vote

third.head: Cold comfort for women
body: Amit Varma has a new measure of women’s empowerment, drawn from a very old observation: the default temperature of office air conditioning.

When air conditioning became common in offices in the 1950s and 60s, he said, it was designed for men in suits. Men have a different metabolic rate and prefer it colder, so a temperature normal for him would be too cold for a woman. {118-S03}
Hence an argument he suspects every married couple has had: the wife says she is cold, and the husband tells her to put on a sweater. {#sweater}
Varma would like the default to rise a little, until men and women are both comfortable. He admitted he does not know how to measure it at scale, and asked viewers for metrics of their own.

p2.title: The hidden heart
p2.deck: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what empowerment metrics, search data, dating apps and Facebook reveal about men and women

sections.label: Empowerment
sections.head: More divorces, please
sections.caption: metrics of empowerment
body: Amit Varma’s starting point was a column he wrote many years ago arguing that India’s rising divorce rates were a good thing. “Rising divorce rates are a sign of women’s empowerment,” he said. {118-S01}

The idea grew into an episode of his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen*, “Metrics of Empowerment”, in which he and three friends hunted for unusual numbers. Solo travel by women was one, and Varma reports it is rising. Nidhi Gupta suggested counting the families whose last child is a boy. Hamsini Hariharan suggested counting women in prison.
## The hand on the phone
Some numbers that sound good can deceive. In traditional families, a man who downloads the BigBasket app may simply hand the phone to his wife to choose the groceries, and pay.

Ajay Shah offered an example from the hosts’ Life Lessons course. Someone decides to have pizza, someone decides on Domino’s, and someone places the order. If the men make the first two decisions, the woman tapping the app shows nothing about her agency. {118-S02}

Even rising incomes can mislead. Women’s participation in India’s labour force rose and then dipped drastically, Varma said, stressing that the causes are many. One is that some families, once they reached a certain income, felt that a working wife “affects the family honour”. {118-C02}
~ Varma asked viewers for empowerment metrics of their own. Two-wheeler and car ownership by women, he noted, are among the standard ones.

quote.text: More women in prisons is a good thing because it means more women have agency

sections.label: The secret self
sections.head: Google Baba knows best
sections.caption: what our searches reveal
body: *Everybody Lies*, Amit Varma said, rests on one idea: people are most truly themselves when they search online, because nobody is watching. It is where, in Gabriel García Márquez’s scheme, the secret self shows.

Its author, Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, drew on anonymised data from Google, Facebook and Pornhub. Facebook itself shows the opposite face: it is, in his words, “digital brag-to-my-friends-about-how-good-my-life-is serum”. {118-J17}
## What the search box hears
The top complaint about marriage, the searches suggest, is a lack of sex. There are 16 times more complaints about a spouse not wanting sex than about one not willing to talk. {118-C04}
Varma stressed that what people search for or fantasise about has nothing to do with what they would want in the real world.

Parents are two and a half times more likely to ask whether a son is gifted than a daughter, though young girls have larger vocabularies and are more often in gifted programmes. Varma imagines the bias is far worse in India. {118-C05}
~ Many of us, he said, never reveal our true selves to anyone, not even to ourselves. And someone who hides that self can never be truly loved. {118-C06}

quote.text: Searches for sexless marriage are three and a half times more common than unhappy marriage, and eight times more common than loveless marriage.

sections.label: The swipe economy
sections.head: A million to choose from
sections.caption: what dating apps tell us
body: Ajay Shah asked the awkward question. Male and female desire, he said, “have probably not changed in 65,000 years”. So what is new? {#years}

Amit Varma, describing rather than endorsing, said a biologist would tell you men are wired to seek youth and beauty, and women status and affluence. In a small circle, ordinary men found partners. On an app, “I have a million people to choose from.” {118-C10}

Marriage, he argued, was an uneasy equilibrium from a time when people met few others: a bundle of love, sex, companionship, friendship and shared parenthood. Nobody has worked out how to live once it is unbundled.
## A cold equilibrium

Varma read a tweet by Rob Henderson, who coined the term luxury beliefs. Men high on the dark triad of psychopathy, narcissism and Machiavellianism, perhaps 10 to 20 per cent of users, mistreat women, who then mistreat ordinary men, who in turn mistreat ordinary women. {118-C11}
~ Many are dropping out. In one survey, Varma said, three in ten men and one in four women had not had sex in a year: a sex recession, as the term now goes. {118-C13}

quote.text: Bad behaviour drives out the good.
quote.who: Rob Henderson, as read by Amit Varma

sections.label: The friendship index
sections.head: Friends by the billion
sections.caption: the When Harry Met Sally index
body: Amit Varma loves *When Harry Met Sally*, a charming film, he said, and he had a crush on Meg Ryan. {118-R24}
Its premise, as Billy Crystal’s character tells Meg Ryan’s, is that men and women can’t be friends, because “the sex part always gets in the way”.

Facebook has now put a number on it. A study of 1.8 billion adult users and 1.4 trillion links between them produced a cross-gender friendship index, which *The Economist* proposed to call the When Harry Met Sally Index.
Varma had been calling it the Whimsy Index, until he realised the I already stands for index: the When Harry Met Sally Index Index. {118-J12}
## Higher than expected

Zero means the sexes are entirely segregated; one means as many friends of the other sex as of one’s own. India scored 0.35, which surprised Varma, given how awkward Indian men are with women. {#india}
Ajay Shah was excited that the data goes down to the smallest administrative units, so researchers could study the separation of the sexes city by city and district by district.

~ Shah also read a passage from Ford Madox Ford’s *Parade’s End*: lovers must wait together “for a week, for a year, for a lifetime” before the final intimate conversation. “Beautiful,” Varma replied. “You have a romantic soul in you.” {118-R27}

quote.text: The purdah that we have in India that the two genders stand apart is something that is just completely broken.

photo.hint: American data scientist, author of Everybody Lies

side.boxText: *Everybody Lies*, by Seth Stephens-Davidowitz, uses anonymised searches to study human nature. Amit Varma called it phenomenal, and read many of its findings from his essay *The Truth About Ourselves*. Its premise: the secret self shows when we search. {118-C03}

contQuote.text: We can never truly know another person. I would argue at one level we can never truly know ourselves. These are the great problems of humanity.

p3.title: Tales from the data
p3.deck: What searches, swipes and a pavement camera say about us

stories.start: this is an experiment you dear readers can carry out yourself
stories.end: So it's absolutely worth trying and there are insights in there.
stories.caption: the Google autocomplete test
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s home experiment with Google autocomplete
stories.head: What husbands want, by country
body: Amit Varma has an experiment you can carry out at home. Open an incognito window, so that Google’s autocomplete is not coloured by what you have searched before, type the start of a sentence and see how the world finishes it. Better still, use a VPN to pretend to be somewhere else.

When Seth Stephens-Davidowitz wrote *Everybody Lies*, the top completion in India of “my husband wants” was a wish to be breastfed. The book reports that porn searches for women breastfeeding men are four times higher in India and Bangladesh than anywhere else. {118-S06}
“I simply don’t get this,” Varma said. He had tried to work out the cultural reasons, and could not.
Times change. When Varma tried it, breastfeeding had slipped to number two. Number one was “my husband wants me to serve his mistress”.

Then he set his VPN to Australia, as he does to watch cycling on SBS. There, husbands wanted an open marriage, a second wife, and something far stranger. One completion was “an open marriage novel”. “Australians want to read books about the things that they are bothered about,” Varma concluded. {118-J05}
Ajay Shah wondered whether VPNs could compare the states of India. Varma’s VPN only does countries, but he thought there might be a research project in it.
~ The point, he said, is that anyone can try this: “you don’t have to be a privileged recipient of anonymised data from Google.”
stories.why: Basic urges are shared, Varma suggested, but culture shapes how they show up. A search box, read country by country, is a free window into private preoccupations, and anyone can open it.
stories.postscript: Also from Varma’s searches: “is my husband gay” is far more popular than “is my husband cheating”.

stories.end: there's that multiplicity of choices. There is a jadedness, no one's happy
stories.caption: Tinder in three cities
stories.kicker: Malini Goyal’s Tinder data, as told by Amit Varma
stories.head: Delhi waits, Bangalore doesn’t
body: For their book *Unboxing Bengaluru*, Malini Goyal and her co-author looked at Tinder data from Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore, measuring how long matched users took to go to each other’s homes.

In Delhi it took months, in Mumbai weeks, in Bangalore days. Amit Varma offered reasons: Delhi is a low-trust society, housing in Mumbai is at a premium, and many singles in Bangalore live alone. {118-S12}
Then Goyal went out and spoke to users. Among them, Varma said, “the promiscuity was off the charts, but nobody was happy”. {#happy}

~ Back in the day, you fell for someone, had an argument, came back and tried to work things through. Today ten other matches are chatting in real time, and if something is mildly wrong with one person, you move on.
stories.why: Building a relationship means working through friction. An app with ten alternatives always waiting makes leaving easier than staying, Varma suggested, and too much choice can leave people jaded rather than happy.

stories.start: So I've had a measurement idea on this subject, uh not implemented it
stories.end: producing daily data for the presence of women in the public square
stories.caption: the camera on the pavement
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s unbuilt measure of women’s freedom
stories.head: Who walks home after dark?
body: Ajay Shah has a measurement idea he has not yet built, but thinks is feasible and worth doing: fix a camera with a telephoto lens outside a window, framed on the pavement.
Code would count the people in the frame and classify their gender. That yields two numbers: the share of people in public who are women, and how that share tails off as evening comes in.

Shah, who has worked on crime victimisation surveys, links it to a question put to parents: what time should their teenage daughter be back home? The answer reflects social mores and how safe parents think the streets are. {#daughter}
~ It is, he said, “a little piece of software that needs to be built”. Then cameras around the world could be “quietly purring”, producing daily data on women in the public square. {118-S04}
stories.why: How many women are out in public, especially after dark, is a simple, continuous measure of how free a society is. With today’s image classifiers, Shah suggested, it is within easy reach.

stories.start: I once wrote a column on how it's immoral to have children
stories.end: if you can call parenting buying or whatever, procreating buying
stories.caption: the regrets of parents
stories.kicker: Amit Varma, a provocative column and the search data
stories.head: Buyer’s remorse in the nursery
body: Amit Varma once wrote a column arguing that it is immoral to have children, partly to be provocative. A lot of parents, he said, got really angry.

Only after reading *Everybody Lies* did he understand why. People are seven times more likely to ask Google whether they will regret not having children than whether they will regret having them. That much, he said, is what you would expect.
The second figure is not. “Adults with children are three point six times more likely to tell Google they regret their decision than are adults without children,” Varma read out. {118-S07}
~ “So full buyer’s remorse happening,” he said, “if you can call parenting buying.” {118-J08}
stories.why: What people say about parenthood in public and what they type alone can be very different. A fierce backlash may be a sign that an argument has touched a private regret.
